title: An afternoon at the New Bilibid Prison

sub_topics: Most surprising reaction to last Sunday's column on subhuman conditions of jails came from ex-convict who had served his 20-year sentence
He reminded CJP of handwritten note he gave during CJP's visit as sitting SC member at New Bilibid Prison (NBP) in Muntinlupa City over a decade ago
SC security team had advised CJP to decline the invitation to visit NBP
However, CJP decided to accept after attending Mass in which Gospel reading was Matthew 25:31-46 -- about Final Judgment, about our Lord asking whether His disciples visited Him when in prison
CJP told himself: 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to risk the ire of the Lord!'
One sunny afternoon, CJP motored to Muntinlupa -- first and only incumbent member of highest court of land to set foot on this notorious home of criminals
CJP pleasantly surprised at sheer size of penitentiary
Imposing, high-walled and barbed-wired was building housing maximum-security inmates
Around this concrete behemoth was vast tract of land planted with fruit trees and shrubs
Ushered to makeshift 'auditorium' on greenery outside forbidding building where some 500 inmates were seated
They broke into thunderous applause while gawking at their visitor
Their prison band played 'Mabuhay' as CJP entered, and Philippine National Anthem to begin convocation
Solemn invocation soon followed
Genuinely entertained by talent show -- especially comedy skit about life in jail, some 20 inmates enlivening program with folk dances and hip-hop
At end, asked CJP to speak
CJP began by asking how many of them had been personally judged by him
About 30 sheepishly raised their hands, to whistles of the rest
Then cautiously asked how many felt they had been wrongly sentenced
To CJP's great relief, saw no raised hand
CJP spoke boldly of hope
Said iron bars may restrict their movements and may subject them to ostracism and ridicule
Nonetheless, they should not hate the world and lose their faith
Explained in Filipino: 'Iba't iba po ang mga kulungan. Dito po sa Muntinlupa, rehas na bakal ang kulungan'
'Ang mas mahirap na kulungan ay ang kulungan ng kaisipan tulad ng mga luko-luko at kulang-kulang'
'Kulungan ng katawan tulad ng mga lumpo'
'At kulungan ng tiyak na kamatayan tulad ng mga may terminal cancer'
'Ang mga kapansanang ito ay higit mahirap harapin'
'Walang gamut para sa kulang-kulang at sa cancer'
'Samantalang ang mga nasa loob ng rehas na bakal ay mayroon laging pag-asa, sapagka't may taning ang kanilang kulungan'
'At maaari pang mabawasan ang sentencia sa pagpapakita ng mabuting asal at pagreporma'
Those imprisoned behind bars have real hope because one day after serving their sentences, they would be freed
With good behavior, penalties could be commuted, or they could even be pardoned
But those imprisoned by greed, by feeble minds, by incurable illness, or by lame bodies could be condemned to pain and suffering all their lives
As CJP ended speech, inmates gave standing ovation
Some of them handed CJP handwritten letters
One gave note in Filipino, CJP now translates to English: 'Isn't it true that all the commandments of the Lord can be summed up in one sentence, Love God and love your fellow beings?'
'Why then did you have to consign me to prison? Contrast this with the way our Church treats sinners'
'After confessing my sins, the priest merely counseled me, then asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me'
'Why didn't you just follow my confessor's example? Why did you have to jail me?'
It was late already, and CJP didn't have time to read his note then
But his letter now begs CJP to answer his decade-old questions
CJP begins with Matthew 25, the Gospel reading that inspired the visit
Here Lord was judging His people, separating sheep from goats, placing 'sheep on His right' and 'goats on His left'
Those who refused to give food to hungry, drink to thirsty, clothe naked, visit sick and imprisoned -- condemned to 'eternal punishment'
Those who did -- promised 'eternal life'
CJP believes that just as there are human and physical laws, there are also spiritual laws
Just as there are consequences for violation of human and physical laws, there are penalties for violation of God's laws
Civil laws protect sanctity of contracts; party who breaks them can be held liable for damages
One who injures another violates criminal laws and is jailed as consequence
Violation of laws of physics impels consequences -- jumps out of window, falls to ground per law of gravity
Similarly, spiritual laws operate on our spirit whether we like it or not
When we transgress Lord's commandments, our spirit suffers consequences by being damned in eternity
Just as there are reparations for violation of human and physical laws, there is also salvation from our sins
By repentance, restitution and reformation -- three Rs of salvation

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second half of his two-part jails series -- a deeply personal field-report-as-pastoral-reflection following E98 (Aug 3) which had described the subhuman conditions of Philippine jails. A gathering of convicts: the most surprising reaction to CJ's column last Sunday came from an ex-convict who had served his 20-year sentence -- he reminded CJ of a handwritten note he gave him during CJ's visit as a sitting member of the Supreme Court at the New Bilibid Prison (NBP) in Muntinlupa City over a decade ago. The SC's security team had advised CJ to decline the invitation to visit the NBP. However, CJ decided to accept it after attending a Mass in which the Gospel reading was Matthew 25:31-46 -- about the Final Judgment, about our Lord asking whether His disciples visited Him when He was in prison. CJ told himself, 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to risk the ire of the Lord!' And so, one sunny afternoon, CJ motored to Muntinlupa -- the first and, as far as he knows, the only incumbent member of the highest court of the land to set foot on this notorious home of criminals. CJ was pleasantly surprised at the sheer size of the penitentiary. Imposing, high-walled and barbed-wired was the building housing the maximum-security inmates; around this concrete behemoth was a vast tract of land planted with fruit trees and shrubs. CJ was ushered to a makeshift 'auditorium' on the greenery outside the forbidding building where some 500 inmates were seated; they broke into thunderous applause while gawking at their visitor. Their prison band played 'Mabuhay' as CJ entered, and the Philippine National Anthem to begin the convocation; a solemn invocation soon followed. CJ was genuinely entertained by the talent show -- especially a comedy skit about life in jail -- and some 20 inmates enlivened the program with folk dances and hip-hop. At the end, they asked CJ to speak. He began by asking how many of them he had personally judged. About 30 sheepishly raised their hands, to the whistles of the rest. Then he cautiously asked how many of them felt they had been wrongly sentenced. To CJ's great relief, he saw no raised hand. CJ spoke boldly of hope. He said that iron bars may restrict their movements and may subject them to ostracism and ridicule, and that nonetheless, they should not hate the world and lose their faith. He explained in Filipino: 'Iba't iba po ang mga kulungan. Dito po sa Muntinlupa, rehas na bakal ang kulungan. Ang mas mahirap na kulungan ay ang kulungan ng kaisipan tulad ng mga luko-luko at kulang-kulang; kulungan ng katawan tulad ng mga lumpo; at kulungan ng tiyak na kamatayan tulad ng mga may terminal cancer. Ang mga kapansanang ito ay higit mahirap harapin. Walang gamut para sa kulang-kulang at sa cancer. Samantalang ang mga nasa loob ng rehas na bakal ay mayroon laging pag-asa, sapagka't may taning ang kanilang kulungan. At maaari pang mabawasan ang sentencia sa pagpapakita ng mabuting asal at pagreporma.' Those imprisoned behind bars, he said, have real hope because one day after serving their sentences, they would be freed; in fact, with good behavior, their penalties could be commuted, or they could even be pardoned -- but those imprisoned by greed, by feeble minds, by incurable illness, or by lame bodies could be condemned to pain and suffering all their lives. Difficult questions: as CJ ended his speech, the inmates gave him a standing ovation; some of them handed him handwritten letters. One of them gave CJ a note in Filipino which he now translates to English: 'Isn't it true that all the commandments of the Lord can be summed up in one sentence, Love God and love your fellow beings? Why then did you have to consign me to prison? Contrast this with the way our Church treats sinners. After confessing my sins, the priest merely counseled me, then asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me. Why didn't you just follow my confessor's example? Why did you have to jail me?' It was late already, and CJ didn't have the time to read his note. But his letter now begs CJ to answer his decade-old questions. CJ will begin with Matthew 25, the Gospel reading that inspired him to visit the NBP. Here, the Lord was judging His people, separating the sheep from the goats, placing 'the sheep on His right' and 'the goats on His left'; those who refused to give food to the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, visit the sick and the imprisoned, He condemned to 'eternal punishment,' and those who did, He promised 'eternal life.' CJ believes that just as there are human and physical laws, there are also spiritual laws -- just as there are consequences for the violation of human and physical laws, there are penalties for the violation of God's laws. For example, civil laws protect the sanctity of contracts, and a party who breaks them can be held liable for damages; one who injures another violates criminal laws and is jailed as a consequence; so too, a violation of the laws of physics impels consequences -- hence, when one jumps out of a window, one falls to the ground in accordance with the law of gravity. Similarly, spiritual laws operate on our spirit whether we like it or not -- when we transgress the Lord's commandments, our spirit suffers the consequences by being damned in eternity; just as there are reparations for violation of human and physical laws, there is also salvation from our sins, by repentance, restitution and reformation -- the three Rs of salvation.
